source.label: Barnhart: Shitao’s last paintings date from “the final decade of his life, between about 1696 and 1707”, settled in Yangzhou
Barnhart: “Flowers held important meanings for Shih-t'ao”

highlight.text: [Shitao] was a true lover of flowers; he [understood] their silent message and knew how to [interpret] the fragrance in poetic and pictorial symbols

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V

source.label: Barnhart catalogue: “Hanging scroll, ink on paper; inscribed by the artist”
Barnhart: “a passionate, wet, exuberant creation”, in ink on paper

work.text: The painting itself is a passionate, wet, exuberant creation of the kind Shih-t'ao painted only after mid-life.

source.author: Richard M. Barnhart
source.title: Peach Blossom Spring: Gardens and Flowers in Chinese Paintings
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

work.text: Whatever the flowers may be, [hibiscus or plum-blossoms, chrysanthemums or epidendrums] by a rockery, a few sprigs of [bamboo], or old banana-leaves, [they are transmuted] into impressions of light and shade, movement and growth, [all] reverberant with life-breath transmitted through the point of the brush

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V

moment.text: This was the period of his “great cleansing,” of the washing away of his earlier identities as Buddhist monk and refugee i-min heir of the Ming imperial family, and the beginning of a settled, secular life, [primarily] in Yangchow, as a professional [painting] master.

source.author: Richard M. Barnhart
source.title: Peach Blossom Spring: Gardens and Flowers in Chinese Paintings
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: As I grow older, I have stopped having lush dreams; Even one hibiscus tree by the pond is too much for me!

source.author: Shitao (Shih-t'ao)
source.title: Inscription on Hibiscus and Lotus
source.publisher: translated by Maxwell K. Hearn in Richard M. Barnhart, Peach Blossom Spring, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1983 (Internet Archive scan)
